lessons.title: Claude Application Design
lessons.summary: The exam checks whether you can pick the right Claude surface for a requirement, design the contracts between your app and Claude (system prompt boundaries, tool and output schemas), and keep sessions and plugins clean. Expect scenarios where several surfaces could work and you must choose the one that fits the constraints with the least custom engineering.
keyPoints: **Surfaces**: claude.ai/Desktop = end-user apps with Anthropic's own system prompt plus Projects, connectors and memory. **Claude Code** = agentic coding in terminal/IDE/desktop. **Messages API / Client SDKs** = you control everything (system prompt, tools, loop, storage). **Agent SDK** = Claude Code's tools, agent loop, permissions, hooks and sessions as a Python/TS library you host. Other languages can drive the same loop with `claude -p --output-format json` as a subprocess.
**Projects do not carry over to the API**: instructions go into `system`, knowledge must be sent (as `document` blocks, via retrieval, or via the Files API).

**The Messages API is stateless by default**: the client stores history and resends `messages` (alternating `user`/`assistant`) every call. In multi-instance backends keep history in shared storage keyed by conversation, not in process memory.
**Local vs remote MCP**: Claude Desktop and Claude Code can launch local stdio servers; claude.ai in the browser and the API's MCP connector reach only remote servers (Streamable HTTP, with auth).
Products built on the Agent SDK must not offer claude.ai login or rate limits without Anthropic's approval. Use API keys or cloud-provider credentials.

**Content boundaries**: the Usage Policy applies on every surface. The system prompt narrows scope, persona and tone within policy. Untrusted content (web pages, emails, tool output) goes in labelled tags as data, and side-effecting tools stay behind approval.

**Schema design**: describe every property (units, formats such as ISO 8601), use `enum` for closed sets, list only truly required fields, and make fields nullable when the source can lack them (otherwise the model fabricates values). `strict: true` and `output_config.format` need `additionalProperties: false` on every object.
**Tool naming**: overlapping or vague tools cause random selection. Merge them or write descriptions that say what each does and when to call it.

**Claude Code sessions**: `/clear` for an unrelated task, `/compact [focus instructions]` to keep going on the same task, `--continue`/`--resume` to come back. After repeated failed corrections, start fresh with a better prompt. Durable conventions go in CLAUDE.md.

**Plugins** bundle skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers (and more) behind a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest. Skills are namespaced `/<plugin>:<skill>`. Scopes: user (`~/.claude/settings.json`), project (committed `.claude/settings.json`; each collaborator still installs), local (`.claude/settings.local.json`). Precedence is local > project > user.

Every enabled plugin puts its skill and agent names and descriptions into context on every turn, and its hooks and MCP servers run as you. Disable unused ones, review third-party plugins before installing, and test your own with `--plugin-dir`.
traps: Expecting the API to remember earlier turns, or to see claude.ai Project knowledge. It sees only what you send.
Using `/compact` when the next task is unrelated. Use `/clear`; compaction carries old noise forward.
Forcing every schema field to be required. When data can be missing, a required string invites invented values.
Assuming a project-scope plugin is installed for teammates once it's committed. It's enabled for them, but each person still installs it.
Putting untrusted retrieved text in the system prompt, which gives it more authority, not less.
Choosing the Agent SDK for a narrow custom-tool agent. If you need no file or shell tools, the Messages API (or tool runner) is the simpler, tighter fit.

code.src:
# Client-held state: rebuild the conversation from your own store each turn
history = store.load(conversation_id)          # list of {role, content}
history.append({"role": "user", "content": user_text})
resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=2048,
    system=SYSTEM_PROMPT,                     # your instructions, not claude.ai's
    messages=history,
)
history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
store.save(conversation_id, history)

lessons.drill: In 15 minutes: (1) Write a 2-turn chat script on the Messages API that deliberately forgets to resend history, see the failure, then fix it with a stored message list. (2) Define an extraction tool with `strict: true`, one nested object and one nullable field. Send it an input missing that field and confirm you get `null`, not an invented value. (3) In Claude Code, run `/plugin`, check which plugins are enabled at which scope, and disable one you don't use.

lessons.title: Software Engineering Foundations
lessons.summary: The exam checks that you can wire Claude into normal production software without breaking basic engineering rules: HTTP semantics (status codes, retries, idempotency, pagination), solid JSON handling, bounded async concurrency against rate limits, and using Claude in git, CI and code review while humans keep control. Most questions describe a real failure (duplicate emails, a 429 storm, a CI job that never runs) and ask which fix goes to the root cause.
keyPoints: **Idempotency**: `POST /v1/messages` is not idempotent. Retrying after a timeout can start a second billed generation. If **your** endpoint has side effects (it writes a row or sends an email), accept a client idempotency key and store the result under it before you add retries anywhere.

**Status codes**: 400 `invalid_request_error`, 401 authentication, 403 permission, 404 not found or model not available, 413 `request_too_large` (fix the request). 429 `rate_limit_error` is **your** quota: honor `retry-after`. 500 `api_error` and 529 `overloaded_error` are server-side: back off and retry.
**Retry only** 429, 5xx/529 and connection errors, with exponential backoff and jitter. Never retry a 400/401/403/404/413 unchanged, because the same request fails the same way.

The official SDKs **already retry** connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and >=500 with exponential backoff (2 retries by default). Tune `max_retries` and `timeout`. Don't wrap another retry loop around the SDK, because the attempts multiply.

**Pagination**: list endpoints (Models, Message Batches, Files) use cursors: `limit`, `after_id`/`before_id`, and responses with `has_more`/`first_id`/`last_id`. SDK list calls auto-paginate when you iterate (`for await` in TS, plain `for` in Python). A cursor stays correct when new items are inserted; an offset doesn't.

**JSON**: parse with a real parser and validate with a schema (Pydantic/Zod). A `tool_use` block's `input` arrives **already parsed** as an object. When you need a guaranteed shape, use structured outputs (`output_config` JSON schema) or `strict` tools instead of regex cleanup.
JSON numbers above 2^53 lose precision in JavaScript. Send large IDs as **strings** in tool schemas and results.

**Async**: use `AsyncAnthropic` (Python) or the promise-based TS client for I/O-bound fan-out. **Bound** concurrency with `asyncio.Semaphore` or `p-limit`, sized to whichever limit binds first (RPM, input TPM or output TPM). A bare `gather`/`Promise.all` over thousands of items causes a 429 storm.
Create the client **once** and reuse it so connections are pooled. Never call a sync client inside an `async def` handler, because it blocks the event loop.
For large jobs that aren't urgent (results within 24 h), the **Message Batches API** is asynchronous and costs 50% less. It usually beats hand-rolled concurrency.

**Claude Code GitHub Actions** (`anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`): quick setup is `/install-github-app`. With no `prompt` input it runs in interactive mode and answers `@claude`. With a `prompt` input it runs in automation mode, for example on every PR. CLI flags go in `claude_args` (`--max-turns`, `--model`, `--allowedTools`). Keep keys in GitHub Secrets, or use OIDC for Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry.

**Code review and refactoring**: the repo-root `CLAUDE.md` carries review criteria and conventions into CI runs. AI review adds to required human approval and tests but doesn't replace them. Before a refactor, have Claude write characterization tests, then change code in small commits on a branch or worktree.
traps: Stacking your own 5-attempt retry on top of the SDK's default retries gives up to 15 HTTP calls per request (5 attempts x 3 SDK tries) during an outage, which makes the outage worse. Use one retry layer.
Reading 429 as an Anthropic outage, or 529 as a problem with your quota. A 429 means your rate limit: slow down. A 529 means server overload: back off and possibly route elsewhere.
Using an unbounded `Promise.all` or `asyncio.gather` and counting on SDK retries to soak up the 429s. Throttle before you send.
Calling `json.loads(block.input)` on a tool_use block. The input is already a dict, so this raises `TypeError`.
Passing `github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` to the action. GitHub doesn't trigger workflows from commits pushed with that token, so CI never runs on Claude's commits.
Putting team conventions in `CLAUDE.local.md` or `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Neither exists on the CI runner; only the committed repo `CLAUDE.md` does.

code.src:
import asyncio
from anthropic import AsyncAnthropic

client = AsyncAnthropic(max_retries=4)  # one retry layer: the SDK's
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(8)              # cap in-flight requests

async def summarize(doc: str) -> str:
    async with sem:
        msg = await client.messages.create(
            model=MODEL_ID, max_tokens=512,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Summarize:\n{doc}"}])
        return next(b.text for b in msg.content if b.type == "text")

async def run(docs):
    return await asyncio.gather(*(summarize(d) for d in docs), return_exceptions=True)

lessons.drill: Write an async script that summarizes 200 short texts, first with an unbounded `gather`/`Promise.all` and then with a semaphore of 5. Log every 429 and its `retry-after` value, and compare the wall-clock time of the two runs. Then iterate a `client.models.list()` call and confirm it pages automatically. Bonus: in a throwaway GitHub repo, run `/install-github-app`, comment `@claude add a README badge` on an issue, and read the workflow log.

lessons.title: Claude API Mechanics
lessons.summary: This sub-skill tests whether you know how the Messages API actually behaves: request shape, stop reasons, streaming events, multimodal input, thinking, prompt caching, batches, files, and what changes on Bedrock, Vertex AI and Foundry. Most questions show a symptom (no cache hits, parse errors, wrong batch mapping) and ask for the mechanical fix.
keyPoints: **Shape**: `model`, `max_tokens`, top-level `system`, `messages` (alternating `user`/`assistant`, starting with `user`), optional `tools`. Content is a string or typed blocks (`text`, `image`, `document`, `tool_use`, `tool_result`, `thinking`). Stateless by default.

**stop_reason**: `end_turn` (done), `max_tokens` (truncated; never execute a `tool_use` from that turn), `stop_sequence`, `tool_use` (run the tools and return `tool_result`s keyed by `tool_use_id` in one user turn), `pause_turn` (a server-tool loop paused; resend including the assistant turn, with no 'continue' message), `refusal` (handle explicitly, read `stop_details`).

**Streaming events**: `message_start`, then per block `content_block_start`, `content_block_delta` (`text_delta`, `input_json_delta`, `thinking_delta`) and `content_block_stop`, then `message_delta` (carries `stop_reason` and usage) and `message_stop`. Accumulate `partial_json` and parse at block stop. Stream long generations to avoid timeouts.

**Vision**: `image` blocks with base64, URL or Files API sources. JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP only. Images before text works best, and larger images cost more tokens. **PDF**: `document` blocks. Each page is sent as extracted text plus a page image, so charts are understood.

**Files API**: upload once, reference by `file_id` across requests. File operations are free, but content is billed as input tokens when used. Not on Bedrock or Vertex AI, where image and PDF sources are base64 only.

**Thinking**: newer models use `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` with `output_config.effort` as the depth knob. Manual `budget_tokens` is rejected on recent models. In tool loops, pass thinking blocks back unmodified. Changing thinking or effort mid-conversation invalidates the messages cache.

**Caching is a prefix match** in render order `tools` > `system` > `messages`. Up to 4 breakpoints. Default TTL is 5 min (refreshed on each read), with `ttl: "1h"` as an option. Writes cost about 1.25x (5 min) or 2x (1 h), reads about 0.1x of base input (some newer models are lower). Below the model's minimum length it silently doesn't cache.

Caching killers: timestamps or UUIDs early in the prompt, non-deterministic JSON, changing tools, switching model. Total input = `input_tokens` + `cache_creation_input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens`.

**Message Batches**: asynchronous, 50% of standard prices (stacks with caching discounts), most batches finish within 1 h, 24 h maximum, up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, results kept 29 days. Results come back in any order, so match on `custom_id`. `errored`, `canceled` and `expired` requests aren't billed. No `stream` in batch requests.
**Realtime vs batch**: a user is waiting, or you need a tool loop: use real-time calls (stream them). Nobody is waiting and the work is bulk (evals, backfills, nightly jobs): use a batch.

**Cloud platforms**: same Messages shape through a platform-specific client with native auth (AWS credentials and region, GCP project and region). Model IDs differ (Bedrock uses `anthropic.` prefixes). Feature parity varies: Anthropic's Batches and Files API aren't on Bedrock or Vertex AI. Check the availability table before you commit.
traps: Putting `cache_control` on the varying last block. Mark the end of the shared prefix instead.
Reading `input_tokens` as the whole prompt once caching is on.
Executing a `tool_use` from a `max_tokens` turn because the partial JSON happened to parse.
Sending "continue" after `pause_turn`, or treating `pause_turn` like `max_tokens`.
Mapping batch results by position instead of `custom_id`.
Porting code to Bedrock or Vertex AI and assuming `file_id`/URL sources, Batches and the Files API come along.
lessons.drill: In 15 minutes: (1) Send the same request twice with a 2,000+ token system prompt marked `cache_control` and print the three usage fields. Then add `datetime.now()` to the top of the prompt and watch reads drop to 0. (2) Stream a tool-using request, log every event type in order, and confirm `stop_reason` arrives on `message_delta`. (3) Submit a 3-request batch with custom_ids `b`, `a`, `c` and map the results back by `custom_id`.

lessons.title: Configuration Management
lessons.summary: Here the exam tests whether you put each piece of configuration in the right place and scope: CLAUDE.md memory files, settings.json scopes and their precedence, pinned model versions versus floating aliases, prompt versioning with change control, and MCP and plugin dependencies. The usual pattern is a team, a personal and an org setting that conflict, and the question asks which one wins or where something belongs.
keyPoints: **CLAUDE.md scopes**: managed policy (org-wide, deployed by IT), user `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (you, every project), project `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` (committed and shared with the team), local `./CLAUDE.local.md` (just you in this project; keep it out of git).

**Loading**: Claude Code loads the CLAUDE.md files in the working directory and every parent directory at launch and **concatenates** them; they don't override each other. CLAUDE.md files in **subdirectories** load on demand, once Claude reads or edits files there.

**Imports**: `@path/to/file`. A relative path resolves from the **importing file**, not the working directory. Imports inside code spans and code blocks are ignored. The first time a project imports something outside the repo, Claude Code asks for approval. Imports help you organize but **don't reduce** context cost.

**What belongs in CLAUDE.md**: build and test commands, conventions, architecture notes, 'always do X' rules, written specifically enough to verify. Aim for under ~200 lines. Move multi-step procedures to **skills** and area-specific rules to `.claude/rules/*.md` with `paths:` frontmatter.
CLAUDE.md is **context, not enforcement**. To guarantee a block, use a permission `deny` rule or a PreToolUse hook.

**settings.json scopes**: user `~/.claude/settings.json`, shared project `.claude/settings.json` (commit it), project local `.claude/settings.local.json` (personal; Claude Code keeps it out of git), and managed.
**Precedence, highest first**: managed > command line (`--settings`) > project local > shared project > user. Nothing in your own files overrides a managed key.

**Array settings** such as `permissions.allow` **merge** across scopes. Scalar keys take the highest-precedence value. `deny` rules beat `allow` rules. Run `/status` to see which settings sources loaded. Settings files are strict JSON, so comments and trailing commas are errors.

**Model pinning**: aliases such as Claude Code's `opus`/`sonnet` point to the recommended version and **change over time**. For reproducible CI and production, pin a full model ID (`--model`, the `model` setting, `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`) or remap an alias with `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL`/`ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL`. Admins restrict choices with `availableModels`.
In API apps, keep the model ID in **one config value per environment** and change it through the same PR, eval and rollout process you use for code.

**Prompt versioning**: treat prompts as code. Keep them in version control with a version ID, log `prompt_version` and the model ID on every request, gate every change with a regression eval, and roll out gradually with a fast rollback.

**MCP scopes**: local (the default, stored in `~/.claude.json`), project (`.mcp.json`, committed, needs approval before use) and user. On a name clash, local beats project beats user, and the winning entry is used whole, not merged. `.mcp.json` expands `${VAR}` and `${VAR:-default}`, so secrets stay out of git.

**Plugins** come from marketplaces (`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`). For a team rollout, commit `extraKnownMarketplaces` and `enabledPlugins` in `.claude/settings.json`. For reproducible installs, pin git-based plugin sources to a `ref` or `sha`. Check marketplaces and plugins with `claude plugin validate`.
traps: Assuming user settings beat project settings. It's the other way round: local > project > user, and managed beats everything.
Expecting a line in CLAUDE.md like 'NEVER edit migrations/' to be enforced. Only permissions and hooks enforce anything.
Committing personal items (sandbox URLs, a preferred model) to the shared CLAUDE.md or settings.json. Use `CLAUDE.local.md` or `settings.local.json` instead.
Splitting a 900-line CLAUDE.md into `@imports` to save tokens. Imported files load in full anyway; use path-scoped rules or skills.
Running production or CI on a floating alias, then being surprised when behavior changes after a release.
Hard-coding credentials in a committed `.mcp.json` instead of using `${VAR}` expansion.
lessons.drill: In a scratch repo, set `model` (or any scalar key) to a different value in each of `~/.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json`. Predict which value wins, then check with `/status` and the startup header. Add `permissions.allow` entries in two scopes and confirm both apply. Then write a CLAUDE.md that `@imports` `docs/conventions.md`, add a `.claude/rules/api.md` with `paths: ["src/api/**"]`, and use `/context` to watch when each one loads.

lessons.title: Understanding Requirements
lessons.summary: This area tests whether you can turn a business request into measurable functional and non-functional requirements, then pick the simplest Claude architecture that meets them. Expect requirements such as latency, throughput, data residency, retention/ZDR, compliance and a cost ceiling, each mapped to a concrete design choice.
keyPoints: **Functional** requirements say what the system does: inputs, outputs, integrations and tools, formats, business rules. **Non-functional** requirements say how well and under which limits: latency, throughput, availability, data residency, retention, compliance, cost and auditability.

Make vague goals measurable. 'Fast' becomes 'p95 time-to-first-token < 1 s'. 'Accurate' becomes '>= 95% on a 300-item labeled eval set'. 'Cheap' becomes '<= $X per month at Y requests per day'. Without numbers you can't evaluate or accept the system.

**Latency levers**: streaming (perceived latency is TTFT), a faster or smaller tier (Haiku-class), lower effort or no extended thinking, shorter outputs (`max_tokens`, concise format), prompt caching for long stable prefixes, and parallel independent calls.

**Throughput**: rate limits are measured in requests per minute plus input and output tokens per minute, per model. Plan capacity (limit increases, queues, backpressure) and load-test **before** launch. Retries don't add capacity.
**Real-time vs batch**: if a user is waiting, use the Messages API with streaming. If results can arrive within 24 h, the Message Batches API saves 50%.

**Cost model**: (input tokens x input rate + output tokens x output rate) x volume. The levers are routing to a cheaper tier, caching shared prefixes, batching, capping output and trimming context. Give each cost estimate with its assumptions and compare it to the ceiling.

**Data residency and cloud fit**: Claude is available through the Claude API and through cloud platforms (Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry). Pick the platform and region that satisfy residency, existing cloud commitments and IAM. The Claude API also has inference-geography controls. A system-prompt instruction **never** satisfies a residency requirement.

**Zero Data Retention (ZDR)** is an arrangement at the organization level, and **not every feature is eligible**. Check that each feature you depend on is eligible before designing around it, and prefer stateless calls.
**Compliance and PII**: minimize and redact before sending, enforce redaction in code (DLP checks), use least-privilege tools, keep audit logs, and put a human in the loop for high-impact actions.

**Architecture choice**: start with the simplest option: one call, then a workflow (prompt chain or routing), and an agent **only** when the steps can't be predicted. Fixed, auditable processes favor workflows with programmatic gates.
When requirements conflict (best quality, lowest cost, sub-second latency), quantify the trade-offs with prototypes or evals and have stakeholders set priorities. Don't resolve it silently.
traps: Treating a nightly or offline job as real-time. Batches cost half as much and remove rate-limit pressure on your interactive traffic.
Optimizing total latency when users complain the app feels slow. Streaming usually fixes how fast it feels.
Defaulting to the most capable model when the requirement is a cost ceiling or high-volume classification. Route by task.
Writing 'keep data in the EU' or 'don't retain data' in a prompt. A prompt can't control where processing happens or how long data is kept.
Assuming an org-level ZDR agreement covers every API feature.
Choosing an autonomous agent for a fixed, regulated process that needs the same steps in the same order every time.

code.src:
# Back-of-envelope check against a monthly cost ceiling.
# Rates come from YOUR rate card (USD per million tokens).
def monthly_cost(req_per_month, in_tok, out_tok, in_rate, out_rate,
                 cached_tok=0, cache_read_rate=0.0):
    uncached = in_tok - cached_tok
    per_req = (uncached * in_rate + cached_tok * cache_read_rate
               + out_tok * out_rate) / 1_000_000
    return per_req * req_per_month

ceiling = 3_000
cost = monthly_cost(900_000, 2_000, 300, in_rate=1, out_rate=5,
                    cached_tok=1_500, cache_read_rate=0.1)
print(f"${cost:,.0f} vs ceiling ${ceiling:,}")  # $1,935 vs ceiling $3,000

lessons.drill: Take this brief: 'Insurance claims team wants AI to triage 40k emails a day, flag fraud and draft replies; EU customers; legal says no data kept.' Write 5 functional and 6 non-functional requirements, each with a number. Map every non-functional requirement to a design choice (platform and region, real-time or batch, model tier, caching, redaction, human review). Estimate monthly cost with made-up rates and say which requirement would force a different architecture if it changed.

lessons.title: Systems Life Cycle
lessons.summary: This area tests whether you run an LLM system like any other production service: evaluate before you ship, roll out in stages, monitor quality and cost as well as errors, and handle model deprecations as planned migrations. Typical questions describe a deprecation notice, a silent quality drop or a cost jump, and ask for the right first step.
keyPoints: **Life cycle**: develop (prompt, tools, eval set), then evaluate offline (golden set, regression suite, rubric-based LLM judge with human spot checks), then a staged rollout (shadow or canary behind a flag), then monitor, then maintain (prompt and model updates, migrations).
**Every change is a deploy**: a new prompt, model ID, tool schema, effort level or `max_tokens` value. Version it, evaluate it, roll it out gradually and keep a one-step rollback.

**Deprecations**: Anthropic announces deprecations with retirement dates, and after retirement requests to that model **fail**. They aren't silently redirected. Inventory every place the model ID is used, start migrating early, and run regression evals on the successor.

**Regression evals before switching models**: run the same test set and compare task quality, format/schema compliance, refusal rate, latency, and **token usage and cost**. Different models can tokenize the same text differently and differ in how much they write.

**After a migration**, re-baseline the prompts. Shouty workarounds written for an older model ('CRITICAL: you MUST...') can make a newer, more instruction-following model overtrigger. Remove them and evaluate again.

**Per-request logging**: request ID (`request-id` header; `_request_id` in the SDKs), model, prompt version, `usage` (input, output and cache tokens), latency (TTFT and total), `stop_reason`, and the error status code. Don't log sensitive content by default.

**Watch the `stop_reason` mix**: a rise in `max_tokens` means outputs are being cut off, and a jump in `refusal` or tool errors is a signal too. Quality regressions still return HTTP 200, so a dashboard of error rates alone misses them.
**Online quality monitoring**: sample production traffic into rubric-based or LLM-judge scoring, tagged by prompt version, and feed failures back into the eval set.
**Usage and cost**: the Console usage and cost pages and the Admin API usage and cost reports give org-wide numbers. Alert on cost per day against budget, 429 and 5xx/529 rates, and p95 latency.

**Claude Code OpenTelemetry**: set `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1` plus `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER`/`OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER` and the OTLP endpoint. Metrics include `claude_code.token.usage` and `claude_code.cost.usage`. Prompts are **redacted unless** `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1`. To enforce it org-wide, put these variables in the managed settings `env`; a repo's `.claude/settings.json` can't enable exporters.
Give support the `request_id` of a failing call. Never send API keys.
traps: Swapping in a newer model ID because 'newer is better', without a regression eval and a staged rollout.
Waiting for the retirement date in the belief that traffic will be routed to a successor automatically.
Monitoring only HTTP success rates. Truncation, refusals and quality drift all come back as 200.
Comparing models on price per token alone and ignoring changes in token counts and output length.
Turning on full prompt and response logging to a third-party backend by default, which leaks PII.
A big-bang rollout with no feature flag, no control group and no rollback path.
lessons.drill: Build a 30-item golden set for a small extraction task. Score it on two Claude model IDs and record accuracy, schema-valid rate, average input/output tokens and p95 latency in a table. Write a one-paragraph go/no-go with a canary plan (percentage, metrics, rollback trigger). Then run Claude Code with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1 OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=console` and find `claude_code.token.usage` in the output.

lessons.title: Technical Fundamentals: SDKs, Retries, Timeouts & Streaming
lessons.summary: The exam treats the SDK as a thin, opinionated wrapper over the REST Messages API. It tests whether you know what the wrapper does for you (retries, timeouts, typed streaming, accumulation) and how to configure it. Expect scenarios about retry storms, hanging calls, SSE parsing bugs, sync calls blocking async servers, and keeping API keys off clients.
keyPoints: SDK = REST wrapper: `client.messages.create()` sends `POST /v1/messages` with `x-api-key`, `anthropic-version` and JSON. The SDK adds typed responses, retries, timeouts and streaming helpers. With raw HTTP you must send `anthropic-version` yourself.

**Auto-retries**: connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and >=500 (including 529 overloaded) are retried with exponential backoff, **2 retries by default** (3 attempts in total). 400/401/403/404/413 are not retried, because they fail the same way every time.

Configure with `max_retries` / `timeout` on the client, or per call with `client.with_options(...)` (Python). The default timeout is **10 minutes**. A timeout raises `APITimeoutError` and is retried according to `max_retries`.

The Python SDK refuses **non-streaming** requests it estimates will take longer than about 10 minutes (large `max_tokens`) and raises `ValueError`. Use `messages.stream()` + `get_final_message()` (TS: `finalMessage()`).

Streaming uses **SSE**: `message_start` -> per block (`content_block_start`, `content_block_delta`..., `content_block_stop`) -> `message_delta` (stop_reason, usage) -> `message_stop`. `ping` events can appear anywhere, and new event types may be added, so ignore unknown events.
`message_delta` usage is **cumulative**: take the last value, do not add them up. Tool input streams as `input_json_delta.partial_json` fragments; join them and parse at `content_block_stop`.
Errors can arrive **inside** a 200 stream (`event: error`, for example `overloaded_error`, which is equivalent to a 529). Status-code-based retry logic never sees these errors.
Low-level `messages.create(stream=True)` gives raw events with **no accumulation**. The `messages.stream()` helper gives `text_stream` and the final message.
Async: use `AsyncAnthropic` in asyncio servers (a sync client blocks the event loop). Cap fan-out with a semaphore. Send work that nobody is waiting on through Batches.
WebSockets vs SSE: the Messages API streams over SSE (one-way, over HTTP). Keep the key on a backend and relay to browsers over SSE or WebSocket from that backend.

`base_url` / `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and a custom `http_client` (proxy) point the SDK at gateways. Platform clients (Bedrock and Vertex packages, for example `anthropic[bedrock]`) keep `messages.create` but use the cloud provider's auth (for example AWS SigV4/IAM) and platform model IDs (for example the `anthropic.` prefix on Bedrock); feature support varies by platform.
Log the `request-id` response header (Python `response._request_id`) for support escalations.
traps: Wrapping the SDK in your own retry loop without setting `max_retries=0` multiplies attempts (5 outer x 3 SDK attempts = 15) during the very overload you are trying to ride out.
Treating HTTP 200 as success while streaming: overloads can arrive as in-stream `error` events after the 200.
Adding up `output_tokens` across `message_delta` events double-counts, because the values are cumulative.
Calling `JSON.parse` on each `partial_json` delta fails; join the fragments first.
Assuming WebSockets reach the Messages API directly from a browser. They don't, and a key in the browser is leaked anyway.
Shrinking `max_tokens` to dodge the 10-minute streaming guard: stream instead.

code.src:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=2, timeout=600.0)

# fail fast on a latency-sensitive path only
fast = client.with_options(timeout=4.0, max_retries=0)

with client.messages.stream(model=MODEL, max_tokens=64000,
                            messages=msgs) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)
    final = stream.get_final_message()  # stop_reason, usage, tool_use blocks
print(final.usage, final._request_id)

lessons.drill: In 15 minutes: (1) Make one streaming request with `curl -N` and label every SSE event you see, including any `ping` events. (2) In Python, stream the same request with `messages.stream()`, print the last `message_delta` usage and compare it with `get_final_message().usage`. (3) Set `max_retries=0` and `timeout=0.5` on one call, trigger an `APITimeoutError`, then confirm that the default client retries it (enable `ANTHROPIC_LOG=debug` to see the attempts).

lessons.title: LLM Fundamentals: Tokens, Windows, Sampling, Thinking & Effort
lessons.summary: This sub-skill checks that your mental model of how Claude generates text is right, because many production bugs come from treating tokens as words, `max_tokens` as an input limit, or temperature as a determinism switch. It also covers the current control levers: adaptive thinking, effort levels, fast mode, and zero-, one- and few-shot prompting.
keyPoints: **Tokens** are sub-word units. The ratio to words or characters varies by language, code and JSON, and **tokenizers can change between model generations**, so the same text can cost more tokens. Measure with `count_tokens` for the target model, never with another vendor's tokenizer.

The **context window** holds everything: tools + system + messages + the generated output (including thinking). Cached tokens still occupy the window. An input that alone exceeds the window gets a 400 'prompt is too long'.

`max_tokens` is a **hard cap on output** (thinking + text + tool calls), not an input allowance. Hitting it gives `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. Treat it as a backstop and set it generously for agentic or high-effort work.

**Next-token prediction**: output is generated one token at a time, so (a) output length dominates latency, (b) tokens already emitted condition what follows and cannot be revised, so ask for reasoning before the verdict, and (c) character-exact tasks are unreliable; check them in code.

**Sampling**: temperature reshapes the next-token distribution, and lower values give less variety, but even low values are **not fully deterministic**. Several recent models **reject** `temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k`. For repeatability, tighten the task, constrain the output, and store decisions.

**Adaptive thinking** (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`): the model decides whether and how much to think. It replaces manual `budget_tokens` on recent models. Thinking tokens are billed as output, and **full** thinking is billed even when only a summary is displayed.

**Effort** (`output_config.effort`: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`; support varies by model) is a **behavioural** signal affecting **all** output tokens, including tool calls, not a hard limit. Lower effort means fewer and terser calls, lower cost and faster responses. **Defaults differ by model**, so set it explicitly and re-sweep after migrations.

**Fast mode** (`speed: "fast"`, supported models only): the same model with faster inference, raising **output tokens per second** (not TTFT) at **premium** pricing. Not available with Batches. Fast and standard speed do not share cached prefixes.

**Zero-shot** is instructions only. **One-shot / few-shot** add examples: 3 to 5 diverse ones, wrapped in `<example>` tags and covering edge cases, are among the strongest ways to fix format and tone. Examples add input tokens, so cache the static examples prefix.
Non-determinism means evals need multiple trials per case, and you should judge distributions rather than a single run.
traps: Raising `max_tokens` to 'fit a bigger document'. It only limits output.
Lowering `max_tokens` to save money truncates thinking and answers. Lower effort instead.
Believing `temperature: 0` guarantees identical output, or sending it to a model that rejects sampling parameters.
Treating effort as a strict token budget, or assuming every model has the same default effort.
Expecting fast mode to fix slow time to first token on huge prompts. That calls for caching, a smaller tier, or lower effort.
Few-shot examples that are all alike: the model copies their length and phrasing.
lessons.drill: Take one representative task. (1) Use `count_tokens` on an English, a Japanese and a JSON version of the same content and note the differences. (2) Run the task 5 times each at effort `low` and `high`, and record output_tokens, latency and correctness. (3) Set `max_tokens` to 300 at high effort and observe `stop_reason`. In two sentences, write down which lever you would use to cut cost and why.

lessons.title: Cost & Token Management: Usage, Caching, Batch & Cost per Task
lessons.summary: Expect calculation questions: you get token counts and per-MTok prices in the scenario and must pick the right total or the cheapest configuration. Underneath the arithmetic, the exam tests caching mechanics (prefix match, breakpoints, TTLs), the batch discount, reading usage fields correctly, and judging spend as cost per completed task.
keyPoints: **Usage fields**: `input_tokens` (uncached remainder), `cache_creation_input_tokens` (written to cache at the write rate), `cache_read_input_tokens` (read at the read rate), `output_tokens` (includes thinking). **Total prompt = input + cache_creation + cache_read.**

**Cost formula**: sum of each token count x its rate per million tokens (MTok). Typical multipliers on base input: **5-minute write 1.25x, 1-hour write 2x, read ~0.1x** (some newer models read even cheaper; take exact prices from the scenario or the pricing page).

**Break-even**: with the 5-minute TTL, 2 requests already pay off (1.25 + 0.1 < 2). With the 1-hour TTL you need at least 3. Reads refresh the TTL at no cost. Pick the TTL by the **start-to-start gap**: under 5 minutes, use 5 minutes; 5 to 60 minutes, use 1 hour; longer, re-warm or accept a miss.

**Caching is a byte-exact prefix match** over `tools` -> `system` -> `messages`. Any change at position N invalidates everything after it. Silent invalidators include timestamps or IDs in the system prompt, unsorted JSON, tool lists built from sets, per-user tool sets, and model switches.

**Breakpoints**: up to 4 `cache_control` markers. Put them at **stability boundaries**: the end of the static system/tools, then the conversation tail. Automatic (top-level) caching marks the last block, which is wrong when the prompt ends in unique per-request content. Below the model's minimum cacheable length, nothing caches, silently.
**Concurrency**: an entry is readable only once the first response starts streaming. For fan-out, send 1 request, wait for its first token, then send the rest.

**Batches**: **50% off every token**, cache reads and writes included (the discounts stack). Most batches finish in under 1 hour, and batches expire after 24 hours. Results come back in any order, so match by `custom_id`. No streaming and no fast mode. Use the 1-hour TTL for shared context.
**count_tokens** (`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens`) gives a model-specific pre-flight count for chunking, routing and budget checks. Pass the same system prompt, tools and content as the real call.
**Order of levers**: changes that don't touch capability first (caching, input and output hygiene, batch), then trade-offs (effort, then model). Change one lever at a time against an eval.
**Cost per completed task** = cost per attempt / success rate, plus the downstream cost of failures. A pricier model can be cheaper per task.
traps: Reading only `input_tokens` and concluding the agent uses barely any context, when the rest came from cache.
A 5-minute TTL on traffic with gaps longer than 5 minutes pays the 1.25x write every time, which is worse than no caching.
Automatic caching on a prompt whose tail is unique: you get writes on every request and no reads.
Expecting 40 simultaneous requests to share a cache entry that does not exist yet.
Assuming batch and cache discounts are mutually exclusive. They stack.
Ranking models by per-token price instead of cost per solved task.

code.src:
def cost(u, p):  # p: $/MTok for each meter
    return (u.input_tokens * p["in"]
            + u.cache_creation_input_tokens * p["write"]
            + u.cache_read_input_tokens * p["read"]
            + u.output_tokens * p["out"]) / 1_000_000

system = [{"type": "text", "text": STATIC_RULES,
           "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h"}}]
# put volatile content (dates, user data) AFTER the breakpoint

lessons.drill: Build a 10-line cost calculator, like the snippet, that takes a usage object and a price table. Send one request with a cached 2,000-token system prompt twice and confirm that the second request shows `cache_read_input_tokens > 0`. Then add `datetime.now()` to the top of the system prompt, rerun, watch reads drop to 0, and compute how much the bug would cost per 10,000 requests at made-up prices.

lessons.title: Model Selection & Trade-offs: Tiers, Pinning, Migrations
lessons.summary: Questions here describe a workload and ask which model tier, which configuration, or which migration step is best. Think in tiers (Opus-class = most capable and most expensive, Sonnet-class = balanced, Haiku-class = fastest and cheapest), pin model snapshots in production, and treat every model change as a migration gated by evals, because generations change the API surface.
keyPoints: **Tier heuristics**: Haiku-class for high-volume, latency-sensitive, checkable work (classification, routing, extraction, sub-agents). Sonnet-class for a balanced speed/intelligence default. Opus-class (and above) for complex reasoning and long-horizon agentic coding.

**Trade-off triangle**: quality, latency and cost. A smaller model usually has a shorter TTFT and faster output, but 'a faster model isn't automatically a faster task' if it needs more turns or tokens. Compare **seconds and dollars per completed task** on your eval.

**Multi-model architectures**: a frontier orchestrator with cheaper workers pays off only when there is real bulk to hand off. Choose the model **per conversation or route, not per turn**: switching mid-conversation starts the cache over (caches are model-scoped). Vary effort within a conversation instead.

**Pinning**: production should run a fixed snapshot ID and upgrade deliberately. Current Claude model IDs, including dateless ones, are pinned snapshots. For older models, aliases pointed to dated snapshot IDs. Watch deprecation notices, because retired models stop serving.

**Breaking changes across recent generations** (examples): sampling params (`temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k`) rejected; `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens}` replaced by `{type: "adaptive"}` + `effort`; **prefilled final assistant turn rejected**, so use structured outputs (`output_config.format`) or instructions; new tokenizers changing token counts; different default effort.

**Migration workflow**: fix the 400-causing changes, re-count tokens, re-tune prompts, **re-sweep effort from the new model's default**, run evals (quality, cost per task, latency), then roll out gradually.

**Stepping down for cost**: sweep effort on the current model first. If low effort passes, try one tier down, reset effort to that tier's default, and re-sweep, one notch at a time against the eval. Also check whether a newer model in the same tier is the cheaper option.
A larger model at low effort can beat a smaller model at high effort on cost per solved task. Price lists don't predict the ranking.
Include the cost of failures (human rework, retries) in model comparisons. It often dominates the token bill.
traps: Choosing the most capable tier 'to be safe' for simple high-volume routing, or the cheapest for deep synthesis.
Per-message model routing inside one conversation, which loses the cache every time the model switches.
Carrying `temperature`, `budget_tokens` or a JSON prefill into a new generation and getting 400s.
Switching 100% of traffic because of public benchmarks without running your own evals.
Leaving effort unset across a migration and being surprised by changes in cost or latency.
Relying on fast mode to fix time to first token: it speeds output tokens per second, not the first token.

code.src:
# Before (older generation)
# temperature=0.2, thinking={"type":"enabled","budget_tokens":6000},
# messages=[..., {"role":"assistant","content":"{"}]

resp = client.messages.create(
    model=PINNED_MODEL_ID,                 # explicit snapshot from config
    max_tokens=16000,
    thinking={"type": "adaptive"},
    output_config={"effort": "medium",     # re-swept on the new model
                   "format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": SCHEMA}},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": doc}],
)

lessons.drill: Pick one of your prompts and build a 10-case mini-eval with a pass/fail checker. Run it on two tiers at two effort levels (4 cells) and record pass rate, output tokens, latency and cost per passing case. Then write a one-paragraph migration note listing the request fields that must change if this prompt used temperature, budget_tokens or a JSON prefill.

lessons.title: Agent Construction with Claude
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you can pick the right way to build an agent (manual loop, Tool Runner, Claude Agent SDK, Managed Agents) from requirements about who runs the loop and who hosts tool execution, and whether you can configure the Agent SDK safely: permissions, hooks, subagents, sessions and limits.
keyPoints: Two independent questions separate the four approaches: **who supplies the harness** (loop + context management) and **who supplies the deployment**. Manual loop = neither; Tool Runner and Agent SDK = harness only (you host); **Managed Agents** = harness **and** hosted per-session sandbox.

**Tool Runner** (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner` / `toolRunner`) lives in the regular Anthropic client SDK. It loops over tools *you* define (`@beta_tool`, `betaZodTool`), with per-turn hooks for approval gates, error interception, result modification, retries and `max_iterations`. No built-in tools, no filesystem, no sandbox.

**Claude Agent SDK** (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) is Claude Code as a library: `query(prompt, options)` drives built-in tools (`Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `Glob`, `Grep`, `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`, `Agent`), permissions, hooks, subagents, sessions, MCP and automatic compaction. It spawns a `claude` CLI subprocess that owns a shell, a working directory and session files on local disk.

**Managed Agents**: create a persisted, versioned **Agent** once (`model`, `system`, `tools`, `mcp_servers`, `skills`), then create a **Session** per run that references it. Updating an agent creates a new version; running sessions keep their pinned version. Extras: scheduled deployments, memory stores, multiagent threads, outcomes (rubric-graded iteration), vaults for credentials.

Managed Agents **self-hosted sandbox** (`config: {type: "self_hosted"}`): the agent loop stays on Anthropic's orchestration layer, tool execution (bash, files, code) moves to your infrastructure; your worker long-polls outbound, Anthropic never dials in. If the *loop itself* must run on your infra, use the Agent SDK or the Client SDK.
Agent SDK permission evaluation order: **hooks -> deny rules -> ask rules -> permission mode -> allow rules -> `canUseTool` callback**. A hook or deny rule can block even in `bypassPermissions`.

`allowed_tools` / `allowedTools` **auto-approves** listed tools; it does not hide the others. `disallowed_tools` with a bare tool name removes the tool. Modes: `default`, `dontAsk` (deny anything that would prompt: good for headless), `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto` (classifier), `bypassPermissions` (isolated environments only; `allowed_tools` does not constrain it).

SDK hooks are in-process callbacks registered under `options.hooks` with a `matcher` on the **tool name** (regex/pipe list such as `"Write|Edit"`). `PreToolUse` returns `permissionDecision` (`allow`/`deny`/`ask`) and optional `updatedInput`; `PostToolUse` can add context or replace output but cannot stop a tool that already ran. Hooks don't consume context.

Subagents: define them in `agents` with `AgentDefinition` (`description`, `prompt`, `tools`, `model`, ...); Claude invokes them through the `Agent` tool. A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context: it gets only its own prompt plus the Agent tool's prompt string, and only its final message returns to the parent.

Sessions: read `session_id` from the result message; `resume` a specific ID, `continue` the most recent, `fork_session` / `forkSession` to branch history (not files). Transcripts live on local disk, so ephemeral containers need a `SessionStore` adapter or app-level state.

Bound every production run: `max_turns` / `maxTurns`, `max_budget_usd` / `maxBudgetUsd` (counts subagent spend). Check the `ResultMessage` `subtype` (`success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_max_budget_usd`, `error_during_execution`) before reading `result`.

Without a `systemPrompt`, or with a custom one, the Agent SDK does not use Claude Code's system prompt; use the `claude_code` preset (optionally with `append`) to get Claude Code's tool-use guidance. Project `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/settings.json` load through `setting_sources` / `settingSources`.
traps: Confusing the **Tool Runner** with the **Agent SDK**: the Tool Runner has no built-in file/bash tools and no permission system; the Agent SDK does. Neither hosts anything for you.

Assuming `allowed_tools=["Read"]` makes an agent read-only. It only pre-approves `Read`; in `bypassPermissions` everything else is approved too. Use `disallowed_tools`, `dontAsk`, or a `PreToolUse` hook.
Putting security checks only in `canUseTool`: calls approved earlier (allow rule, `acceptEdits`, `bypassPermissions`) never reach it. Put must-run checks in a `PreToolUse` hook.
Expecting a `Write|Edit` matcher to protect a file: matchers match tool names, so a `Bash` redirect bypasses it. Match `Bash` too, add deny rules, or sandbox the filesystem.
Calling `agents.create()` on every request in Managed Agents. Create once, store the ID, update with `POST /v1/agents/{id}` (new version), and start sessions per run.
Believing the self-hosted sandbox option moves the agent loop on-prem. It moves tool execution only; tool inputs and outputs still flow to Anthropic so the model can see them.
lessons.drill: Build the same tiny bug-finding agent twice: (1) with the Tool Runner and two custom tools (`read_file`, `run_tests`) you write yourself; (2) with the Agent SDK using `allowed_tools=["Read","Grep","Bash"]`, `permission_mode="dontAsk"`, a `PreToolUse` hook on `Bash` that denies `rm`, and `max_turns=15`. Run both, capture the SDK `session_id`, then `resume` it with a follow-up prompt and `fork_session=True` with another. Write down which features you had to build yourself in version (1).

lessons.title: Agent Patterns & Frameworks
lessons.summary: This sub-skill covers the mechanics inside any agent: the tool-use loop, how results flow back, how to keep context healthy over long runs (subagents, context editing, compaction, memory), and how third-party frameworks such as Strands Agents, LangGraph and Pydantic AI fit around Claude.
keyPoints: The loop: call the Messages API with `tools` -> if `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, run each `tool_use` block -> append the **full** assistant `response.content`, then one user message with a `tool_result` per call (matching `tool_use_id`) -> repeat until `end_turn`. Handle `max_tokens`, `pause_turn` and `refusal` explicitly, and cap iterations.
Parallel tool use is on by default: return **all** `tool_result` blocks for a turn in a **single** user message. Splitting them across messages teaches Claude to stop making parallel calls.
Tool failures: return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and an actionable message so Claude can retry or adapt. Never drop the result (the next request is invalid) or crash the loop.
`pause_turn` (server-side tools hit their internal iteration limit): re-send the conversation with the assistant content as-is; don't add a "Continue" user message.
Promote an action from `bash` to a **dedicated tool** when you need to gate, render, audit or parallelize it: a `send_email` tool is easy to gate; `bash -c "curl ..."` is opaque to the harness.

**Subagents** isolate context: each runs in its own window and returns only a condensed result, so the orchestrator's context grows by a summary, not a transcript. Costs: extra tokens, latency and coordination; poor fit for tightly coupled steps that need shared state.

**Context editing** (`clear_tool_uses_20250919`, `clear_thinking_20251015`) clears stale tool results/thinking without summarizing. **Compaction** summarizes earlier context server-side near a threshold; you must append the full `response.content` (including the compaction block) each turn. **Memory** is for persistence **across** sessions.

The **memory tool** (`memory_20250818`) is client-side: Claude issues `view`/`create`/`str_replace`/`insert`/`delete`/`rename` on a `/memories` directory and *your* handler stores it. No built-in access control: use per-user directories, never store secrets.

In the Agent SDK, compaction is automatic (a `compact_boundary` system message marks it); durable rules belong in `CLAUDE.md` (re-injected every request), and a `PreCompact` hook can archive the full transcript first.

**Strands Agents** (AWS, open source): model-driven agent loop, `@tool` decorator, Amazon Bedrock is the default provider, Claude via Bedrock or the `AnthropicModel` provider (Anthropic API); multi-agent patterns include agents-as-tools, swarm, graph and workflow; MCP support; deploys to AgentCore, Lambda, containers.

**LangGraph**: low-level orchestration runtime; you build a graph of nodes and edges over shared state, mixing deterministic and LLM steps. Strengths: durable execution with checkpointing, human-in-the-loop interrupts, short- and long-term memory, streaming. Does not require LangChain; Claude usually comes in via `ChatAnthropic` (`langchain-anthropic`).

**Pydantic AI**: typed Python agent framework. `output_type` validates results against Pydantic models and asks the model to retry on validation failure; `deps_type` + `RunContext` inject dependencies into tools; `@agent.tool`; model chosen by string such as `anthropic:...`; OpenTelemetry/Logfire, durable execution, evals, and tool-approval support.
traps: Appending only the assistant's text (not the full `content` list) to history: you lose `tool_use` blocks (next `tool_result` is orphaned -> 400) and compaction blocks.
Using compaction or context editing as "memory": both work **within** a session. Cross-session recall needs the memory tool, files, or a store.
Assuming more subagents always means better results: each adds tokens and latency, and subagents only know what you put in their prompt.
Treating a framework as a reason not to understand the prompts and tool calls underneath. Anthropic's guidance: start with the API, and if you use a framework, know what it sends.
Thinking LangGraph or Strands are Claude-specific or Anthropic-hosted. They are third-party, multi-provider frameworks you run yourself; Claude is one model provider among many.
Ending the loop on `stop_reason != "tool_use"` without checking `max_tokens`: a truncated answer gets reported as complete.
lessons.drill: Write a manual tool-use loop (no Tool Runner) with two tools, one of which randomly throws. Make it return `is_error` results, batch parallel results in one user message, cap iterations at 10 and handle `max_tokens`. Then add the memory tool with a per-user `/memories/<user_id>` directory and check that a fact saved in run 1 is recalled in a fresh run 2. Finally, sketch (on paper) the same agent as a LangGraph graph and as a Pydantic AI agent with an `output_type`, noting what each framework would take over.

lessons.title: Agent Architecture
lessons.summary: This sub-skill is about choosing the simplest architecture that works: a single call, one of the five workflow patterns from "Building effective agents", or an autonomous agent, possibly with an orchestrator and workers. Expect scenarios that ask you to name the pattern, spot over-engineering, and weigh cost, latency and error recovery.
keyPoints: **Workflows** run LLMs and tools through predefined code paths; **agents** let the LLM dynamically direct its own process and tool use. Start with the simplest solution (often one well-prompted call with retrieval and examples) and add complexity only when it measurably helps.

**Prompt chaining**: sequential calls, each consuming the previous output, with optional programmatic **gates** between steps. Trades latency for accuracy on tasks that split cleanly into fixed steps (outline -> check -> draft).

**Routing**: classify the input, then send it to a specialized prompt, tool set or model (e.g. refunds vs technical support; easy queries to Haiku, hard ones to Opus). Separation of concerns; the classifier can be an LLM or a traditional model.

**Parallelization**: **sectioning** splits a task into independent subtasks run at once (e.g. a guardrail screen running alongside the main response); **voting** runs the same task several times for diverse outputs or higher confidence (e.g. several vulnerability-review prompts).

**Orchestrator-workers**: a central LLM decides the subtasks at runtime, delegates them and synthesizes results. The key difference from parallelization is that the subtasks are **not predefined** (e.g. which files a change touches).

**Evaluator-optimizer**: one LLM generates, another critiques against clear criteria, in a loop. Use it only when evaluation criteria are clear and feedback measurably improves the output; always cap iterations.

Build an agent only if the task is complex and hard to specify in advance, valuable enough to justify cost and latency, within Claude's ability, and errors can be caught and recovered from (tests, review, rollback). If any answer is no, stay with a workflow.

Agents need ground truth from the environment at each step (tool results, test runs), human checkpoints for risky actions, and stopping conditions (max iterations, budget). Autonomy raises cost and the risk of compounding errors: test in sandboxes.

Supervisor/orchestrator hierarchies: workers get isolated contexts and only the brief you give them, so brief them with objective, scope boundaries, tools and output format; they return condensed results. Cap depth, concurrency and spend; use cheaper models for reading-heavy workers and a capable model for planning and synthesis.

Three principles from Anthropic: keep the design simple, make the agent's planning transparent, and invest in the agent-computer interface (clear tool docs, poka-yoke parameters such as requiring absolute paths).
traps: Calling any fan-out "orchestrator-workers". If the subtasks are fixed in code before the input arrives, it is parallelization (sectioning).
Reaching for a multi-agent supervisor when a routing workflow or a single call with retrieval meets the requirement. Over-engineering is the most common wrong answer.
Using evaluator-optimizer without explicit criteria: the loop oscillates and burns tokens. Add a rubric and an iteration cap, or drop the pattern.
Adding voter or checker agents to every answer of a high-volume Q&A flow "for accuracy": each pass multiplies cost. Prefer better context, higher effort and cheap deterministic checks.
Re-running an entire chain when one step fails. Validate at gates and retry the failing step with the error as feedback.
Assuming parallel workers share what they learn. Each worker sees only its brief, so overlapping or vague briefs produce duplicated and missed work.

code.src:
import asyncio

async def review(code: str):
    # Parallelization (sectioning): independent checks run at once
    sec, perf, style = await asyncio.gather(
        ask(SECURITY_PROMPT, code), ask(PERF_PROMPT, code), ask(STYLE_PROMPT, code))
    # Programmatic gate before the next chain step
    if not all(r.ok for r in (sec, perf, style)):
        raise ValueError("A reviewer returned malformed output")
    return await ask(SUMMARY_PROMPT, f"{sec.text}\n{perf.text}\n{style.text}")

For each, estimate model calls per request and name the main failure mode. Pick the simplest one that meets a stated quality bar and justify it in two sentences, as you would on the exam.

lessons.title: Prompt Engineering
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you can turn a vague or brittle prompt into one Claude follows reliably: explicit instructions with the reason behind them, structured inputs, well-chosen examples, and an eval loop to prove a change helped. It also checks that you know which old idioms (assistant prefill, shouting in capitals) are obsolete or harmful on current models, and how to keep untrusted text from being read as instructions.
keyPoints: **Be clear and direct**: state audience, goal, output format and constraints explicitly. The doc's test: if a colleague with minimal context would be confused by the prompt, Claude will be too.
**Give the why**: context or motivation behind a rule ("output is read by a text-to-speech engine, so never use ellipses") lets Claude generalise beyond the literal rule.

**Examples (few-shot)** are among the most reliable steering tools: make them relevant, **diverse** (cover edge cases, vary surface form so Claude does not copy unintended patterns) and wrap them in `<example>` tags inside `<examples>`. The docs suggest 3–5.
**XML tags** (`<instructions>`, `<context>`, `<input>`, `<document>`) separate instruction from data and reduce misinterpretation. Tag names are not magic keywords; consistency matters more.
**Role** goes in the `system` prompt. Even one sentence ("You are a senior tax accountant…") focuses tone and expertise.

**Long context (20k+ tokens)**: put documents at the **top**, the query and instructions at the **end** (up to ~30% quality gain in Anthropic tests). Wrap each document in `<document>` with `<source>` and `<document_content>` subtags, and ask for relevant quotes first.

**Prefill is gone on current models**: a trailing assistant turn returns a 400 on the 4.6-and-later generations. Replace JSON-forcing prefills with `output_config.format`, label-forcing with an enum tool or schema, and preamble-skipping with a system instruction. Assistant turns *earlier* in `messages` (few-shot history) are still fine.
**Format control**: say what to do, not what to avoid ("write flowing prose paragraphs" beats "no markdown"), and match your prompt's own style to the output you want.
Current models follow instructions closely, so old "CRITICAL: you MUST" emphasis can cause **over-triggering**. Dial it back to normal phrasing.

**Iterate with evals**: define success criteria, build a test set including edge cases, grade automatically where possible (code checks, then LLM graders with clear rubrics), change one thing at a time and compare versions before shipping.

**Untrusted input**: deliver third-party content in `tool_result` blocks (or clearly tagged, JSON-encoded user content), never in `system`. State in the system prompt that such content is data, and screen it with a lightweight model when risk is high. Prompt wording alone is not a security boundary.
traps: Moving a working prefill to a newer model unchanged. It returns a 400, it does not just get ignored.
Thinking all assistant messages are banned. Only a **trailing** assistant turn is a prefill; few-shot user/assistant pairs that end with a user turn are fine.
Five near-identical examples. Claude copies their length, phrasing and structure. Diversity beats volume.
Putting the question first and a 100-page document after it. For long inputs, documents go first and the query goes last.
Interpolating user or web text into the system prompt "so it gets more attention". That gives attacker-controlled text operator authority.
Judging a prompt change by eyeballing two outputs, or tuning against the same examples you then evaluate on.

code.src:
resp = client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=2048,
    system="You are a contracts analyst for a mid-size SaaS company.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": (
        f"<documents>\n<document><source>msa_v3.pdf</source>\n"
        f"<document_content>{contract}</document_content></document>\n</documents>\n\n"
        "First quote the clauses relevant to termination in <quotes> tags. "
        "Then answer in <answer> tags: can we terminate for convenience, and with what notice? "
        "Legal reviewers read this, so cite clause numbers for every claim."
    )}],
)

docs.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

lessons.drill: Take a prompt you use in production. (1) Write 10 test inputs, 3 of them edge cases, plus a pass/fail check for each. (2) Rewrite the prompt: role in `system`, inputs in XML tags, long data first and query last, one sentence of motivation per rule, and 3 diverse `<example>`s. (3) Remove any trailing assistant prefill and use `output_config.format` instead. Run both versions on all 10 cases and compare pass rates.

lessons.title: Context Engineering
lessons.summary: Context is a finite attention budget. The exam tests whether you keep the window full of high-signal tokens as an agent runs for a long time. Expect scenarios where you must pick between clearing old tool results, summarising (compaction), delegating to subagents, retrieving just in time, and persisting notes or memory across sessions.
keyPoints: **Context rot**: as token count grows, the model's ability to recall and use any given piece of context drops, even well under the hard limit. Aim for the **smallest set of high-signal tokens** that gets the job done.

**Budgeting**: input plus output must fit the model's context window. Measure with the token counting endpoint (`messages.count_tokens`) or read `usage.input_tokens` from responses rather than guessing from characters.

**Tool-result pruning at the source**: tools should return only the fields the agent needs, support filtering and pagination, and truncate with a hint about how to fetch more. A 40k-token raw API dump wastes budget on every later turn.

**Context editing** (`clear_tool_uses_20250919`, beta `context-management-2025-06-27`) **prunes** old tool results server-side, replacing them with a placeholder. Parameters: `trigger` (default 100k input tokens), `keep` (default 3 recent tool uses), `clear_at_least`, `exclude_tools`, `clear_tool_inputs`. Your client keeps the full history.
Clearing changes the prompt prefix, so it **invalidates the prompt cache** from that point. Use `clear_at_least` so each clear frees enough tokens to justify the new cache write.

**Compaction** (`compact_20260112`) **summarises** earlier context into a `compaction` block when input approaches a trigger. You must append the full `response.content` (including that block) to history, not just the text.

Pick by need: editing for stale tool output within a session, compaction for conversations that will outgrow the window, memory for state that must survive across sessions. Long-running agents often use all three.
**Subagents** give isolation: each explores in a clean window and returns a condensed summary (the engineering post cites roughly 1,000–2,000 tokens), so the lead agent's context stays small.

**Just-in-time retrieval**: keep lightweight identifiers (paths, queries, URLs) and load data through tools when needed. **Hybrid** is common: Claude Code loads `CLAUDE.md` up front and uses glob and grep to pull files on demand.

**Memory and notes**: the memory tool (client-side, `/memories` directory) or a NOTES.md-style file lets an agent persist progress outside the window. Combined with context editing, Claude is warned to save important information before results are cleared.
When writing your own compaction prompt, tune for **recall first** (keep decisions, open bugs, key details), then precision (drop redundant tool output).
traps: "The window is 1M tokens, so load everything." Context rot makes stuffing worse even when it fits.
Confusing context editing (deletes old tool results, no summary) with compaction (writes a summary). The exam tests which fits a scenario.
Appending only the response text after compaction. The `compaction` block is lost and the next request resends the full history.
Forgetting that each clear invalidates the cached prefix. Small, frequent clears can cost more than they save.
Having subagents return their full transcripts to the orchestrator. That defeats the isolation.
Treating context editing or compaction as cross-session memory. Both work within one conversation; persistence needs memory files or a store.

code.src:
resp = client.beta.messages.create(
    model=MODEL, max_tokens=8000,
    betas=["context-management-2025-06-27"],
    tools=tools,
    messages=messages,
    context_management={"edits": [{
        "type": "clear_tool_uses_20250919",
        "trigger": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 60000},
        "keep": {"type": "tool_uses", "value": 4},
        "clear_at_least": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 10000},
        "exclude_tools": ["get_requirements"],
    }]},
)

docs.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

lessons.drill: Build a small agent loop with a `read_file` tool over a repo of about 50 files and ask it to audit every file. Log `usage.input_tokens` per turn. Then add `clear_tool_uses_20250919` with `keep: 3` and `clear_at_least`, and compare the token curve and cache-write tokens. Finally move the per-file audit into a subagent call that returns a 200-word summary, and compare again.

lessons.title: Output Handling
lessons.summary: Model output is untrusted until your code has checked it. The exam tests constraining format with structured outputs and strict tools, checking `stop_reason` before you touch content, parsing and validating defensively, and verifying fluent, confident claims against sources.
keyPoints: **JSON outputs**: `output_config: {format: {type: "json_schema", schema}}` uses constrained decoding so the response matches the schema. SDK helpers (`messages.parse()` with Pydantic or Zod) also validate and return typed objects.
**Strict tool use**: `strict: true` on a tool definition guarantees schema-valid tool names and inputs. It replaces "retry until the arguments parse" loops.

Schema limits: `additionalProperties: false` on every object. Recursive schemas and numeric or string-length constraints (`minimum`, `maxLength`) are unsupported and return a 400 if sent raw. The Python and TS SDK helpers strip them and validate client-side instead.
A new schema pays a one-time grammar compilation latency, then it is cached (24 hours from last use).
**Schema-valid is not correct.** Structured outputs guarantee shape, not truth. Still apply business rules (totals add up, IDs exist, dates are in range).

**Check `stop_reason` first**: `end_turn` means normal completion. `max_tokens` means truncated, so JSON may be incomplete or a `tool_use` input may be a valid-looking partial object; do not execute it, retry with a higher limit. `refusal` means the output may not match your schema; branch on it before parsing.
Do not assume `content[0]` is text. With thinking or tools, find blocks by `type`.

**Defensive parsing** when structured outputs aren't available: strict parse, then validate with a schema library. On failure, retry with the validation error as feedback or route to a fallback. Never `eval()`, and do not regex-grab the first `{...}`.

**Citations** make claims auditable: enable on document blocks and each text span carries the cited passage. Citations are **incompatible** with `output_config.format` (400). Prefill is also incompatible with JSON outputs.

**Scepticism toward confident output**: give Claude permission to say "I don't know", ground answers in direct quotes, have it retract claims it cannot support with a quote, restrict it to the provided documents, and use best-of-N comparison to spot inconsistencies. Always validate critical facts.
traps: Wrapping `json.loads` in a retry loop when the real cause is `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`. Truncation is the bug; raising the limit or chunking is the fix.
Executing a `tool_use` from a `max_tokens` turn because its input parsed. Truncated input often parses as a valid partial object.
Treating a 200 response as success. A `refusal` is a 200 with a non-schema body.
Believing structured outputs make extracted values correct. They only make them well-formed.
Turning on citations and `output_config.format` together in one request. It is rejected; choose one, or use the documented citations-with-structured-data pattern.
Trusting a confident, well-formatted answer with specific numbers or section references. Fluency is not evidence; check grounding.
lessons.drill: Write an invoice extractor two ways: (a) prompt-only "return JSON" with `json.loads`, and (b) `output_config.format` plus Pydantic or Zod validation. Feed both 20 invoices, including one very long invoice with a deliberately small `max_tokens` and one with line items that do not sum to the total. Make sure (b) branches on `stop_reason` and flags the business-rule failure instead of crashing or silently accepting it.

lessons.title: Tool Implementation
lessons.summary: The exam tests whether you can define tools Claude will pick correctly, wire the tool_use/tool_result loop without protocol errors, and design tool outputs and approval gates that hold up in production. Expect scenarios about bad descriptions, broken parallel-result handling, error reporting, server vs client tools, and scaling to large tool sets.
keyPoints: A client tool is `name` + `description` + `input_schema` (JSON Schema). The **description matters most**: say what the tool does, what it returns, and **when to call it**. Describe every parameter; use `enum` for fixed values; name params unambiguously (`user_id`, not `user`).

Loop contract: response has `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and one or more `tool_use` blocks. Append the full assistant `content`, run the tools, then send ONE `user` message with a `tool_result` per `tool_use_id`. `tool_result` blocks must come **first** in that content array; any text goes after them.
Parallel tool use: Claude may emit several `tool_use` blocks in one turn. Every one needs a matching `tool_result` in the very next user message. A missing or split result returns a 400.

Tool failure: return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and an **actionable** message (what failed, what to try next). Don't throw out of the loop, and don't pass a failure off as an empty success.

`strict: true` on a tool constrains inputs to the schema (objects need `additionalProperties: false`). It guarantees structure, not business rules: numeric limits such as `minimum`/`maximum` aren't enforced by the grammar.

`tool_choice`: `auto` (default) or `none` work everywhere. Forced modes (`any`, `{type:"tool"}`) are rejected with a 400 on some of the newest models. Portable pattern: `auto` plus a prompt instruction, `strict: true`, and a check-and-retry if no call was made, or structured outputs (`output_config.format`) when the call only existed to get JSON. `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` caps it at one call per turn.

Server tools (web search, web fetch, code execution, tool search) run on Anthropic's infrastructure. You get back `server_tool_use` + result blocks, never return a `tool_result` for them, and on `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` you resend the conversation including the paused assistant content, with no added "Continue" message.
Client tools are executed by your code. That covers your custom tools and Anthropic-defined but client-executed tools (bash, text editor, memory, computer use). You host any sandbox.

Approval gates: put them in code, not the prompt. With the SDK Tool Runner, gate inside the tool's run function (return a "user declined" result) or inspect the yielded tool call before it runs. Hard-to-reverse actions are the classic candidates.
Promote an action from bash to a **dedicated tool** when the harness must gate, render, audit, or parallelize it. A typed `send_email` is easy to intercept; `bash -c "curl ..."` is not.

Large tool sets: add the tool search tool and set `defer_loading: true` on most tools. Keep the 3 to 5 most-used tools and the search tool itself non-deferred (all-deferred returns a 400). Selection accuracy degrades past roughly 30 to 50 loaded tools.

"Writing tools for agents": consolidate multi-step chains (`schedule_event` over `list_users` + `list_events` + `create_event`), prefer search over list, namespace tools (`jira_search`), return semantic fields instead of raw UUIDs, offer `response_format` concise/detailed, and paginate/filter/truncate with sensible defaults that tell the agent how to narrow its query.
traps: Sending each parallel `tool_result` in its own user message. All results for one assistant turn go in a single user message.
Putting a text block ("Here are the results:") **before** the `tool_result` blocks. That is a 400. Text may only follow the results.
Treating forced `tool_choice` as the portable way to guarantee a call. Newer models can reject it. Use `auto` + `strict` + verify, or structured outputs for extraction.
Returning a `tool_result` for a `server_tool_use` id, or appending "Continue." after `pause_turn`. Both are wrong.
Relying on a system-prompt instruction ("ask before refunds") as an approval control. Only code that runs before execution is a gate.
Silently truncating big tool outputs. Say that output was truncated and how to narrow the query, or the agent will reason from partial data.
lessons.drill: Write two client tools (`get_order`, `refund_order`) and a manual loop. 1) Ask a question that triggers two parallel `get_order` calls and confirm both results go back in ONE user message. 2) Make `get_order` raise for one ID and return `is_error: true` with a helpful message, then watch Claude recover. 3) Gate `refund_order` behind an input() approval that returns "declined by user" when rejected. 4) Put a text block before the tool_result to see the 400, then fix the order.

lessons.title: Agentic Customization
lessons.summary: This sub-skill is about picking the right extension point. You choose among built-in/server tools, custom tools, Agent Skills, MCP servers, subagents, hooks, CLAUDE.md, and plugins, based on what has to load when, who needs to reuse it, and whether it must be deterministic. Most questions are "which mechanism BEST fits" scenarios where several options would technically work.
